title: Five Historical Novels Every Child Should Read Before High School
author: Restoring the West
summary: This piece argues that historical fiction is an essential tool for helping children escape presentism—the tendency to judge past peoples and events through a modern critical lens—and that older novels written before 1970 are best suited to this purpose. The author recommends five works spanning the English colonial era through the Civil War: Johnny Tremain by Esther Forbes, Carry On Mr. Bowditch by Jean Lee Latham, Little House in the Big Woods or Farmer Boy by Laura Ingalls Wilder, Across Five Aprils by Irene Hunt, and Amos Fortune Free Man by Elizabeth Yates. Each recommendation is annotated with a brief description and appropriate age range. The article argues that historical fiction cannot replace primary sources or quality textbooks but can help students understand and empathize with past generations by providing a window into the values, customs, and traditions that shaped earlier Americans. L.P. Hartley's observation—'The past is a foreign country; they do things differently there'—frames the conclusion that great books function as passports helping children access and appreciate the generations that came before them.
points: Historical fiction can help children escape presentism—judging past people through a critical modern lens—in ways that primary sources and textbooks alone cannot accomplish.

Older historical novels written before 1970 are best suited to this purpose because they were written by authors who had not yet absorbed the assumptions that make the past feel alien to current readers.
The five recommended novels span key American historical periods: colonial Boston, early maritime America, 19th-century pioneer life, the Civil War, and 18th-century New England slavery.
Historical fiction piques student interest in specific time periods and events, serving as a gateway to deeper study rather than a replacement for it.

L.P. Hartley's axiom—'The past is a foreign country; they do things differently there'—is truer today than ever as accelerating cultural change makes even the 20th century feel alien to contemporary students.
quotes: In order for American children to understand history, they must first learn to appreciate the values, customs, and traditions of past generations. This can best be done through historical fiction, which gives students a window into places, people, and ideas that are very different from their own experiences.
Historical fiction can also pique a student's interest in a particular time period or event.
Older historical novels—particularly those written before 1970—are best at this.
These books, set respectively in the woods of Wisconsin and upstate New York, give children a glimpse into the hard work, resourcefulness, and fortitude of ordinary 19th century Americans.
Novelist L. P. Hartley wrote that 'The past is a foreign country. They do things differently there.' His statement is truer today than ever.

The accelerating change in our culture now means that even the 20th century seems alien to today's students. But good books—especially historical literature—can be a passport to the past, helping students understand and empathize with the generations of Americans that came before them.
